points: A cache keeps a copy of data closer to the reader than the source of truth, so most reads skip the slow path.
The price is staleness: every write has to reach the cache too, by invalidating the old entry or letting it expire.
Races between reads, writes and invalidations can leave the cache holding a value the database no longer has.
Uber built its cache inside the database and used the database's own change log as the signal to invalidate entries.
Meta measures cache consistency by what a client could actually observe, and notes that rare bugs tend to hide in error-handling paths.

prerequisiteReasons.load-balancing: Load balancing spreads requests across servers, and a cache then lowers the load further by answering reads before they reach the source of truth.

points: Consensus is how a group of replicas agree on one value, or one order of values, even though machines crash and messages are lost.
A leader appends each change to a replicated log, and a change counts as committed once a majority has stored it.
Any two majorities overlap, so the system can lose a minority of nodes and still agree.
The cost is a round trip to that majority on every write, so consensus trades latency for agreement.
The etcd guide says commit latency has a floor set by the network round trip between members plus a durable disk write.

prerequisiteReasons.cap: CAP names the trade between consistency and availability, and consensus is how a strongly consistent system stays available while a quorum survives.
prerequisiteReasons.replication: Consensus keeps replicas agreeing on one order of changes, so you first need to know what replicas are and why every change must reach them.
